rossgetman@aol.com (RossGetman) schrieb im Nachricht <19990122212437.09410.00001254@ng-fb1.aol.com>:

>
>"Robert" points out that Kaczynski
>in ISAIF Para. 18 states what he
>describes as the "leftist" approach:
>
>"Thus if a person is 'inferior' it 
>is not his fault, but society's, because he has 
>not been brought up properly."
>
>In his diary, Kaczynski spoke of his
>own feelings of inferiority, and
>attributed it to his having not been up properly.
>
>"Suppose that for a period of years 
>whenever you touched -- let us say -- a banana, you got a severe electric
>shock. After that you would always be nervous around bananas, even if you
>knew
>they weren't wired to shock you.  Well, in the same way, the many rejections,
>humiliations and other painful influences that I underwent during adolescence
>at home, in high school, and at Harvard have conditioned me to be afraid of
>people."
>		Letter from Ted Kaczynski		
>
>Rather than blaming himself for
>having a maladjusted personality, he 
>blames his personality defects on society,
>and on his not having been brought
>up properly.   
>
>How many here think that TK is
>responsible for his own problems,
>and how many think it is society's
>fault or on his not having been 
>brought up properly?

This is an interesting question.  Certainly
one may plausibly argue either view, so
perhaps it may be best to say:  Yes.  On
the whole, I'd question the utility of becoming
too absorbed in applying the concept of 
responsibility to his actions, or anyone's 
actions, for that matter.  Responsibility is
a construct which we find useful when trying
to assign blame; in trying to decide who to
punish; or in deciding, perhaps, who must
take action in order to change the situation.
But if we should merely want to appreciate
the interrelationships of the parties involved,
and how their actions are interwoven and
condition each other, then the idea of 
responsibility is not so useful, it seems to me.
For example, if a hammer strikes a nail, and
the nail is driven into two boards, joining
them together, is it the nail or the hammer
that is responsible for the boards being nailed
together?  Both?  Neither?  A third party,
in this case the agency of the man wielding
the hammer, could plausibly be blamed, yet
his actions, too, presumably had a cause.

The problem of responsibility is thus bound up
with the concept of free will.  Only if the actions
of men are completely free does it make
much sense to assign blame or responsibility,
in other than a short term, sociologically 
convenient sense.

Yet if the actions of the man are completely
free, this would seem, in extremis, to be 
equivalent to saying that they are random.
If they are truly random and uncaused, then
even the man himself would not be able to
predict what he will do next, nor why he will
do it.  This situation is inimical to the assignment
of responsibility too.  It may be freedom, but
it's an odd sort of freedom; someone in that
state of mind would certainly appear insane
to us, and so would be relieved of responsibility
for his actions.

However, if the man acts according to a rational
plan, or even according to what we call human
or even animal nature, then his actions will
be predictable, and causation will again be
introduced, abolishing responsibility and
freedom.

Hence, although useful at times to us, it is
easy to see that the idea of personal 
responsibility for one's actions is quite 
a limited one in its utility.  It has some
rather severe epistemological problems.

>
>How many think it was the 
>incident, at six months,
>when he was tied down for 
>hives for a week -- at a time

He seems to have another theory, 
which you quote, above.
